cards.q: What is OSPFv2 and what is its administrative distance?
cards.a: OSPF (Open Shortest Path First, RFC 2328) is an open-standard link-state IGP for IPv4. Routers exchange LSAs to build a shared LSDB, then each router independently runs Dijkstra's SPF to compute the shortest-path tree. Its AD is 110.

cards.q: How does link-state routing differ from distance-vector routing?
cards.a: Link-state (OSPF) routers hold a full topology map (LSDB) and run SPF to compute a guaranteed acyclic loop-free tree with fast deterministic convergence. Distance-vector (RIP/EIGRP-ish) routers only know neighbor distance vectors and rely on split-horizon/holddown tricks for loop safety with slower, potentially unstable convergence.

cards.q: What are the three OSPF tables and their show commands?
cards.a: Neighbor table (adjacent routers and state, show ip ospf neighbor), LSDB (all LSAs, show ip ospf database), and routing table (best SPF routes, show ip route ospf).

cards.q: What is the OSPF hello and dead interval on broadcast and point-to-point networks?
cards.a: Hello is sent every 10 seconds. Dead interval is 4 times the hello, so 40 seconds by default. On NBMA networks hello is 30 seconds and dead is 120 seconds.

cards.q: What multicast addresses does OSPF use?
cards.a: 224.0.0.5 for all OSPF routers, and 224.0.0.6 for DR/BDR on broadcast networks. On NBMA networks OSPF uses unicast. The protocol number is 89.

Cost = reference-bandwidth / interface-bandwidth, with a default reference bandwidth of 100 Mbps. Path cost is the sum of outgoing interface costs. On fast links both 100 Mbps and 1 Gbps cost 1, so auto-cost reference-bandwidth 1000 is often set to keep fast links distinct.

cards.q: Write the basic OSPFv2 configuration in both network mode and interface mode.
cards.a: Network mode: router ospf 1, router-id 1.1.1.1, network 10.0.0.0 0.0.0.255 area 0. Interface mode: interface Gi0/1, ip ospf 1 area 0.

cards.q: What does the passive-interface command do in OSPF?
cards.a: It suppresses hello packets on the specified segment, so no neighbor adjacency forms there, while the network is still advertised.

cards.q: A neighbor is stuck in INIT/2WAY, what is the likely cause and check?
cards.a: Likely a mismatch in hello/dead timers, area ID, or network type. Check with show ip ospf interface to verify these parameters match on both sides.

cards.q: What is the classic cause of flapping OSPF neighbors?
cards.a: MTU mismatch between the two sides - this is a major exam topic. Verify MTU is equal on both interfaces.

cards.q: What is the OSPF NBMA hello/dead timer pair?
cards.a: Hello 30 seconds, dead 120 seconds (4x hello), on NBMA frame-relay style networks, compared to the 10/40 broadcast and point-to-point pair.

cards.q: Does the OSPF network command use a subnet mask or a wildcard mask?
cards.a: It uses a wildcard (inverted) mask, not a subnet mask. For example network 10.0.0.0 0.0.0.255 area 0 uses the wildcard 0.0.0.255.

cards.q: What is the default cost reference bandwidth in OSPF and why does it matter?
cards.a: The default reference is 100 Mbps, so 100 Mbps, 1 Gbps, and 10 Gbps links all compute a cost of 1 and are indistinguishable. Set auto-cost reference-bandwidth 1000 to keep fast links distinct.

cards.q: What is OSPF's RFC, type, and default reference bandwidth?
cards.a: RFC 2328, a link-state IGP, with default reference bandwidth of 100 Mbps, AD 110, port 89, and multicast 224.0.0.5/.6.
